newsitem.title: HAITI: United Nations ponders pullout from Haiti.
newsitem.headline: United Nations ponders pullout from Haiti.

text.p: The head of the United Nations mission in Haiti said on Wednesday he was optimistic that U.N. peacekeepers would leave as scheduled on July 31 despite Canada's announcement that its soldiers would stay until the end of the year.
"The Haitian National Police is making much progress and we are still shooting for the July 31 deadline," U.N. Special Representative Enrique Ter Horst told Reuters.

A wave of violence has left 50 people dead in two months. But Ter Horst said the internationally trained police force --set up in 1995 to replace a repressive and corrupt military --was curbing gangs who have terrorised the population.

U.N. Secretary General Koffi Annan said in a March 24 report to the Security Council that any assessment of the need for further mandate extensions was premature. The question should be addressed again in June, he said.
Despite that report, Canadian Foreign Minister Lloyd Axworthy said after meeting Haitian President Rene Preval last week that Canadian troops would stay until year's end.
Diplomats said the early timing of the Axworthy announcement was due to a meeting planned in Washington between Canadian Prime Minister Jean Chretien and President Bill Clinton on Friday.
"The idea is to go to Washington with an understanding already established between the Canadian government and President Rene Preval," one diplomat said.
Canada is providing 736 troops for the mission of 1,287 U.N. peacekeepers. Nearly 600 troops are provided at Canadian expense, estimated at $8 million per month.
Security in Haiti is of more immediate importance to the United States, which bears the brunt of any flow of boat people and drugs from the impoverished Caribbean nation.
"One could say they owe us one," said Canadian Ambassador to Haiti Christopher Poole.

Washington and Ottawa are at odds over Cuba, with the United States seeking to ostracize the communist-ruled island and Canada playing a leading role in foreign trade and investment there which it hopes might promote political change.

Diplomatic sources said Canada's decision to leave its troops in Haiti until year's end might not give it freer rein in its trade with Cuba but it would be a significant bargaining chip in other bilateral concerns.
Ter Horst agreed that the Axworthy announcement was likely tied to the upcoming Washington meeting.
Any extension of the U.N. mandate would require approval by the U.N. Security Council. Both the Russian and Chinese members have been reluctant to approve past extensions.

Preval promised that his November request for a continued U.N. presence of 8-12 months would be his last mandate extension request. The Security Council granted Haiti an eight-month extension, ending July 31.

Preval does not need to make a formal request to raise a Security Council vote for an extension until the end of November, which would be included within the parameters of his orginal request for up to 12 months.
To extend the mission to Dec. 31, however, Preval would need to break his promise and make a new request.

The peacekeeping mission is comprised of Canadian troops patrolling Haiti's south and Pakistani troops in the north. Some 300 civilian police trainers from French-speaking countries and Creole-speaking Haitian Americans are working in police stations throughout the country.
